108	def load_device(config: dict) -> dict:
109	    """Resolve config['device'] to a manifest dict.
110	
111	    If device.manifest_path is set, it points at a device.json written by
112	    backend/load_blend.py (bpy runs there, in its own venv, against a .blend
113	    + materials.json sidecar — see backend/load_blend.py and
114	    progress_simulation.md step 6). This function only reads that JSON; it
115	    never imports bpy, so the openEMS side stays out of the bpy venv.
116	    Inline device fields (if any) are layered on top of the loaded manifest.
117	    """
118	    device = config.get("device", {})
119	    manifest_path = device.get("manifest_path")
120	    if not manifest_path:
121	        return device
122	    import json
123	    manifest = json.loads(Path(manifest_path).read_text())
124	    return {**manifest, **{k: v for k, v in device.items() if k != "manifest_path"}}
125	
126	
127	@dataclass
128	class FDTDStructure:
129	    """Bundles what run_fdtd/postprocess need. Not part of the frontend
130	    contract -- purely an internal hand-off between the three stages."""
131	    FDTD: object
132	    port: object
133	    nf2ff: object
134	    sim_path: str
135	    freq: object = None  # set by run_fdtd() after CalcPort
136	
137	
138	def build_ifa_geometry(candidate: Candidate, band: Band, device: dict, sim: SimOptions) -> FDTDStructure:
139	    """Step 3/6: ground plane + short pin + radiating arm as CSXCAD PEC
140	    primitives, fed by an openEMS lumped port. Bare PEC only, no
141	    dielectrics yet -- that's step 6, once device['components'] carries
142	    real material data from a Blender export (backend/load_blend.py).
143	
144	    Geometry convention (see IFA_* constants above): candidate.position_mm
145	    is the short-circuit (grounded) pin location; candidate.feed_point_mm
146	    is the feed location, its z giving the pin height (falls back to
147	    IFA_HEIGHT_MM if 0). If the two collapse to the same (x, y) -- true of
148	    the current frontend candidate generator, which has no separate
149	    short-point field -- the short pin is nudged IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM away so
150	    CSXCAD gets two distinct conductors. The radiating arm runs from the
151	    short pin, continuing past it (away from the feed) for length_mm.
152	    """
153	    import numpy as np
154	    openems_env.setup()
155	    from CSXCAD import ContinuousStructure
156	    from openEMS import openEMS
157	
158	    board = device.get("board", {}) if device else {}
159	    # board thickness/stackup is unused here -- bare PEC ground plane only
160	    # until step 6 (dielectrics from the Blender export) fills it in.
161	    board_w, board_l, _ = board.get("size_mm") or [100.0, 50.0, 1.6]
162	
163	    f_low = band.f_low_ghz * 1e9
164	    f_high = band.f_high_ghz * 1e9
165	    f0 = (f_low + f_high) / 2.0
166	    # The Gaussian excitation must stay broadband even when the *reported*
167	    # band is narrow (progress_simulation.md chose a narrow GPS-L1 sweep
168	    # for a fast first pass). A narrow excitation pulse is LONG in the time
169	    # domain and makes the FDTD run slower, not faster -- narrowing the
170	    # reported band is a post-processing lever (fewer CalcPort frequency
171	    # points), not an excitation one. Reuse the ~0.5 f0/fc ratio from
172	    # openEMS's own Simple_Patch_Antenna tutorial rather than deriving fc
173	    # from the (possibly very narrow) band width.
174	    fc = 0.5 * f0
175	
176	    h = candidate.feed_point_mm[2] if candidate.feed_point_mm[2] > 0 else IFA_HEIGHT_MM
177	    short_xy = np.array(candidate.position_mm[:2], dtype=float)
178	    feed_xy = np.array(candidate.feed_point_mm[:2], dtype=float)
179	
180	    # Arm direction is derived from the board, not from the feed/short
181	    # vector: it points from the board centre through the short pin,
182	    # continued outward-to-inward reversed (i.e. from the short pin toward
183	    # the board interior). Deriving it from feed-short instead (as a first
184	    # cut did) is circular once short/feed collapse to one point below --
185	    # the nudge direction would silently become the arm direction too, and
186	    # for an edge-placed candidate that can point the arm straight off the
187	    # board into free space.
188	    center = np.array([board_w / 2.0, board_l / 2.0])
189	    outward = short_xy - center
190	    if np.linalg.norm(outward) < 1e-6:
191	        outward = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
192	    arm_dir = -outward / np.linalg.norm(outward)
193	    perp_unit = np.array([-arm_dir[1], arm_dir[0]])
194	
195	    if np.allclose(short_xy, feed_xy):
196	        # Candidate has no dedicated short-point field. The feed MUST land
197	        # on the arm's centreline (offset along arm_dir, toward the open
198	        # end) so its top actually touches the arm conductor -- an offset
199	        # perpendicular to the arm (a first cut did this) leaves the feed
200	        # pin's top floating in free space next to the arm, not on it,
201	        # which drives nothing: the port sees near-total reflection at
202	        # every frequency (this is exactly what the first real run showed:
203	        # S11 flat at -0.05 dB, VSWR 314, across the whole band).
204	        feed_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM
205	
206	    open_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * candidate.length_mm
207	    perp = perp_unit * (IFA_ARM_WIDTH_MM / 2.0)
208	
209	    mesh_div = 10.0 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 20.0
210	    mesh_res_mm = (C0 / f_high / 1e-3) / mesh_div         # lambda/N at f_high
211	    margin_mm = (C0 / f_low / 1e-3) / 4.0                  # >= lambda/4 at f_low
212	
213	    NrTS = 15000 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 30000
214	    FDTD = openEMS(NrTS=NrTS, EndCriteria=1e-4)
215	    FDTD.SetGaussExcite(f0, fc)
216	    FDTD.SetBoundaryCond([sim.boundary] * 6)
217	
218	    CSX = ContinuousStructure()
219	    FDTD.SetCSX(CSX)
220	    mesh = CSX.GetGrid()
221	    mesh.SetDeltaUnit(1e-3)  # working unit: mm
222	
223	    mesh.AddLine('x', [-margin_mm, board_w + margin_mm])
224	    mesh.AddLine('y', [-margin_mm, board_l + margin_mm])
225	    # Explicit lines at 0 and h: the pins/arm (h = a few mm) are much
226	    # smaller than mesh_res_mm (tens of mm), so the general lambda/N mesh
227	    # alone would never place a line at the pin-top height -- the whole
228	    # pin would fall inside one coarse z-cell with no line bracketing its
229	    # top, which is exactly what caused the lumped port to fail to snap
230	    # to the grid ("Dimension is: 0") on the first run of this geometry.
231	    mesh.AddLine('z', [-margin_mm, 0, h, h + margin_mm])
232	
233	    # metal_edge_res inserts extra lines flanking each conductor edge (the
234	    # openEMS "thirds rule" refinement) -- without it, AddEdges2Grid only
235	    # adds a line exactly at the primitive's own boundary, which is not
236	    # enough to bracket a zero-width pin/port with usable cells either.
237	    edge_res = mesh_res_mm / 2.0
238	
239	    ground = CSX.AddMetal('ground')
240	    ground.AddBox(priority=10, start=[0, 0, 0], stop=[board_w, board_l, 0])
241	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=ground, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
242	
243	    short_pin = CSX.AddMetal('short_pin')
244	    short_pin.AddBox(priority=10,
245	                      start=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], 0],
246	                      stop=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], h])
247	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=short_pin, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
248	
249	    arm = CSX.AddMetal('radiator_arm')
250	    arm.AddBox(priority=10,
251	               start=[short_xy[0] - perp[0], short_xy[1] - perp[1], h],
252	               stop=[open_xy[0] + perp[0], open_xy[1] + perp[1], h])
253	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=arm, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
254	
255	    port = FDTD.AddLumpedPort(1, 50, [feed_xy[0], feed_xy[1], 0],
256	                               [feed_xy[0], feed_xy[1], h],
257	                               'z', 1.0, priority=5, edges2grid='xy')
258	
259	    mesh.SmoothMeshLines('all', mesh_res_mm, 1.4)
260	
261	    nf2ff = FDTD.CreateNF2FFBox()
262	
263	    import tempfile
264	    sim_path = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix=f"openems_{candidate.candidate_id}_")
265	
266	    return FDTDStructure(FDTD=FDTD, port=port, nf2ff=nf2ff, sim_path=sim_path)
267	
268	
269	def run_fdtd(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band, sim: SimOptions) -> FDTDStructure:
270	    """Step 5: run the FDTD solve, then CalcPort over the band's
271	    frequency window (sim.freq_points samples across
272	    [band.f_low_ghz, band.f_high_ghz]) to populate S-parameter data on
273	    structure.port. This is the slow step -- typically minutes even at
274	    sim.mesh_res == "coarse"; see progress_simulation.md step 7 for the
275	    runtime knobs.
276	    """
277	    import numpy as np
278	    structure.FDTD.Run(structure.sim_path, verbose=3, cleanup=True)
279	
280	    n = max(sim.freq_points, 3)
281	    freq = np.linspace(band.f_low_ghz * 1e9, band.f_high_ghz * 1e9, n)
282	    structure.port.CalcPort(structure.sim_path, freq)
283	    structure.freq = freq
284	    return structure
285	
286	
287	def postprocess(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band) -> dict:
288	    """Step 5: S11 curve -> resonant_ghz / bandwidth_mhz / vswr /
289	    s11_min_db from the port data run_fdtd() populated. peak_gain_dbi and
290	    efficiency need an NF2FF run at the resonant frequency (radiated vs.
291	    accepted power); sar_w_per_kg stays 0.0 until a tissue phantom exists.
292	    """
293	    import numpy as np
294	    port = structure.port
295	    freq = structure.freq
296	
297	    s11 = port.uf_ref / port.uf_inc
298	    s11_db = 20.0 * np.log10(np.abs(s11))
299	    s11_curve = [{"f_ghz": float(f / 1e9), "s11_db": float(db)}
300	                 for f, db in zip(freq, s11_db)]
301	
302	    i_min = int(np.argmin(s11_db))
303	    s11_min_db = float(s11_db[i_min])
304	    resonant_ghz = float(freq[i_min] / 1e9)
305	    gamma = min(float(np.abs(s11[i_min])), 0.999)
306	    vswr = (1.0 + gamma) / (1.0 - gamma)
307	
308	    below = s11_db <= band.s11_db_max
309	    bandwidth_mhz = float((freq[below].max() - freq[below].min()) / 1e6) if below.any() else 0.0
310	
311	    efficiency = 0.0
312	    peak_gain_dbi = -99.0
313	    if s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max:
314	        # Coarse angular grid for speed; nf2ff needs a resonance to probe.
315	        theta = np.arange(-180.0, 180.0, 10.0)
316	        phi = np.array([0.0, 90.0])
317	        nf2ff_res = structure.nf2ff.CalcNF2FF(structure.sim_path, freq[i_min], theta, phi)
318	        p_rad = float(nf2ff_res.Prad[0])
319	        p_acc = float(port.P_acc[i_min])
320	        if p_acc > 0:
321	            efficiency = max(0.0, min(1.0, p_rad / p_acc))
322	        dmax_db = float(nf2ff_res.Dmax[0])
323	        peak_gain_dbi = dmax_db + 10.0 * np.log10(efficiency) if efficiency > 0 else dmax_db - 99.0
324	
325	    meets = s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max and efficiency >= band.efficiency_min
326	
327	    return {
328	        "s11_curve": s11_curve,
329	        "s11_min_db": s11_min_db,
330	        "resonant_ghz": resonant_ghz,
331	        "bandwidth_mhz": bandwidth_mhz,
332	        "efficiency": efficiency,
333	        "peak_gain_dbi": peak_gain_dbi,
334	        "vswr": vswr,
335	        "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0,  # stub -- needs a tissue phantom, see progress_simulation.md step 5
336	        "meets_requirements": meets,
337	        "notes": f"resonance {resonant_ghz:.4f} GHz, S11 {s11_min_db:.1f} dB"
338	                 + ("" if meets else " (below thresholds)"),
339	    }
340	
341	
342	def run_simulation(config: dict) -> dict:
343	    """Single entry point the FastAPI backend calls. See
344	    rf/progress_simulation.md for the config/result contract (mirrors
345	    frontend/src/lib/types.ts Candidate/BandRequirement -> SimResult)."""
346	    t0 = time.time()
347	    cand = Candidate(**config["candidate"])
348	    band = Band(**{k: config["band"][k] for k in
349	                   ("id", "f_low_ghz", "f_high_ghz", "s11_db_max", "efficiency_min")
350	                   if k in config["band"]})
351	    sim = SimOptions(**config.get("sim", {}))
352	    device = load_device(config)
353	
354	    try:
355	        structure = build_ifa_geometry(cand, band, device, sim)
356	        port_result = run_fdtd(structure, band, sim)
357	        metrics = postprocess(port_result, band)
358	        result = SimResult(
359	            candidate_id=cand.candidate_id,
360	            status="complete",
361	            runtime_s=time.time() - t0,
362	            **metrics,
363	        )
364	    except NotImplementedError as e:
365	        result = SimResult(
366	            candidate_id=cand.candidate_id,
367	            status="failed",
368	            runtime_s=time.time() - t0,
369	            s11_curve=[], s11_min_db=0.0, resonant_ghz=0.0, bandwidth_mhz=0.0,
370	            efficiency=0.0, peak_gain_dbi=0.0, vswr=0.0, sar_w_per_kg=0.0,
371	            meets_requirements=False, notes=f"not runnable yet: {e}",
372	        )
373	    return result.to_dict()
374	
375	
376	if __name__ == "__main__":
377	    # Tutorial checkpoint (step 2/4): bare IFA over a 100x50mm ground plane,
378	    # no dielectrics, narrowed GPS L1 sweep (1565-1585 MHz) chosen in
379	    # progress_simulation.md for a fast first pass.
380	    demo_config = {
381	        "candidate": {
382	            "candidate_id": "gps_l1_ifa_demo",
383	            "antenna_type": "IFA",
384	            "position_mm": [95, 25, 0],
385	            "feed_point_mm": [95, 25, 5],
386	            "length_mm": 42.6,
387	            "orientation": "edge",
388	        },
389	        "band": {"id": "gps_l1", "f_low_ghz": 1.565, "f_high_ghz": 1.585,
390	                  "s11_db_max": -8, "efficiency_min": 0.45},
391	        "device": {"board": {"size_mm": [100, 50, 1.6]}},
392	        "sim": {"mesh_res": "coarse", "boundary": "MUR", "freq_points": 11},

Here's a structure proposal — not implementing yet, just laying it out for review.

## Proposed layout

```
rf/
├── __init__.py            # new: exposes `from rf import run_simulation`
├── requirements.txt
├── progress_simulation.md
├── openems_env.py         # unchanged — DLL-path setup for CSXCAD/openEMS
├── models.py              # new: Candidate, Band, SimOptions, SimResult, FDTDStructure,
│                           #      Vec3/Bbox, C0, IFA_* constants — everything currently
│                           #      at the top of run_simulation.py
├── device.py               # new: load_device() (reads backend-produced device.json)
├── geometry.py              # new: build_ifa_geometry()
├── solve.py                 # new: run_fdtd()
├── postprocess.py           # new: postprocess()
├── run_simulation.py        # slimmed down: run_simulation() orchestrator + __main__ CLI demo only
├── validate_dipole.py        # unchanged — PyNEC oracle
├── bench_scaling.py          # unchanged — PyNEC oracle
├── vendor/                   # unchanged, gitignored
├── .venv/                    # unchanged, gitignored
└── backend/                  # moved here from top-level backend/
    ├── requirements.txt      # bpy
    ├── load_blend.py         # unchanged
    ├── .venv/                # unchanged, gitignored — separate bpy env
    └── out/                  # generated device.json + STLs, gitignored
```

Each new file's job, one line: `models.py` = data shapes only, no logic; `device.py` = the bpy-adjacent hand-off reader; `geometry.py` = CSXCAD construction; `solve.py` = the FDTD run + `CalcPort`; `postprocess.py` = turning port/nf2ff data into the `SimResult` dict; `run_simulation.py` = wires those four together + the CLI demo, nothing else.

## Two things worth deciding before I implement

1. **Naming collision.** You called this folder "backend" when it sat next to `frontend/`, but "the backend" in this project also means the future FastAPI service (built by the other teammate, per earlier conversation). Once it's `rf/backend/`, those are two different things with the same name. Options: keep `backend/` as-is, or rename to something like `rf/geometry_ingest/` or `rf/blend_loader/` to avoid confusion once the FastAPI service exists.
2. **Invocation convention.** Splitting into sibling modules means `geometry.py`/`solve.py`/etc. need to import `models.py` etc. The clean way is relative imports (`from .models import ...`) plus always invoking via `python -m rf.run_simulation` instead of `python rf/run_simulation.py` — the current file has a try/except shim to support both styles, which would otherwise have to be repeated in every new module. I'd drop the shim and standardize on `-m` (docs/progress_simulation.md's Setup commands get updated to match).

"""Data shapes shared across the sim pipeline. No logic here — geometry.py,
solve.py, postprocess.py and run_simulation.py all import from this module;
it must never import any of them back.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Vec3 = tuple[float, float, float]
Bbox = tuple[Vec3, Vec3]

C0 = 299_792_458.0

# IFA geometry conventions -- Candidate (frontend/src/lib/types.ts) has no
# dedicated short-pin field, so these fill the gap. Documented here rather
# than buried in geometry.py so they're easy to find and revisit.
IFA_HEIGHT_MM = 5.0       # pin height used when feed_point_mm.z is 0
IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM = 3.0    # short-to-feed spacing when position_mm and
                          # feed_point_mm collapse to the same (x, y)
IFA_ARM_WIDTH_MM = 2.0    # radiating-arm strip width


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    candidate_id: str
    antenna_type: str  # "IFA" first; see progress_simulation.md
    position_mm: Vec3
    feed_point_mm: Vec3
    length_mm: float
    orientation: Literal["edge", "corner", "face"] = "edge"
    keepout_mm: Bbox | None = None


@dataclass
class Band:
    id: str
    f_low_ghz: float
    f_high_ghz: float
    s11_db_max: float = -8.0
    efficiency_min: float = 0.45


@dataclass
class SimOptions:
    mesh_res: Literal["coarse", "fine"] = "coarse"
    boundary: Literal["MUR", "PML_8"] = "MUR"
    freq_points: int = 21


@dataclass
class SimResult:
    candidate_id: str
    status: Literal["queued", "running", "complete", "failed"]
    runtime_s: float
    s11_curve: list[dict]  # [{"f_ghz": ..., "s11_db": ...}, ...]
    s11_min_db: float
    resonant_ghz: float
    bandwidth_mhz: float
    efficiency: float
    peak_gain_dbi: float
    vswr: float
    sar_w_per_kg: float
    meets_requirements: bool
    notes: str

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "candidate_id": self.candidate_id,
            "status": self.status,
            "runtime_s": self.runtime_s,
            "s11_curve": self.s11_curve,
            "s11_min_db": self.s11_min_db,
            "resonant_ghz": self.resonant_ghz,
            "bandwidth_mhz": self.bandwidth_mhz,
            "efficiency": self.efficiency,
            "peak_gain_dbi": self.peak_gain_dbi,
            "vswr": self.vswr,
            "sar_w_per_kg": self.sar_w_per_kg,
            "meets_requirements": self.meets_requirements,
            "notes": self.notes,
        }


@dataclass
class FDTDStructure:
    """Bundles what solve.py/postprocess.py need. Not part of the frontend
    contract -- purely an internal hand-off between the pipeline stages."""
    FDTD: object
    port: object
    nf2ff: object
    sim_path: str
    freq: object = None  # set by solve.run_fdtd() after CalcPort

"""Resolves config['device'] to a manifest dict."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from pathlib import Path


def load_device(config: dict) -> dict:
    """If device.manifest_path is set, it points at a device.json written
    by rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py (bpy runs there, in its own venv,
    against a .blend + materials.json sidecar — see
    rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py and progress_simulation.md step 6). This
    function only reads that JSON; it never imports bpy, so the openEMS
    side stays out of the bpy venv. Inline device fields (if any) are
    layered on top of the loaded manifest.
    """
    device = config.get("device", {})
    manifest_path = device.get("manifest_path")
    if not manifest_path:
        return device
    manifest = json.loads(Path(manifest_path).read_text())
    return {**manifest, **{k: v for k, v in device.items() if k != "manifest_path"}}

"""Builds the openEMS/CSXCAD structure for a candidate IFA."""
from __future__ import annotations

import tempfile

from . import openems_env
from .models import (
    C0,
    IFA_ARM_WIDTH_MM,
    IFA_HEIGHT_MM,
    IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM,
    Band,
    Candidate,
    FDTDStructure,
    SimOptions,
)


def build_ifa_geometry(candidate: Candidate, band: Band, device: dict, sim: SimOptions) -> FDTDStructure:
    """Step 3/6: ground plane + short pin + radiating arm as CSXCAD PEC
    primitives, fed by an openEMS lumped port. Bare PEC only, no
    dielectrics yet -- that's step 6, once device['components'] carries
    real material data from a Blender export (rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py).

    Geometry convention (see IFA_* constants in models.py): candidate.
    position_mm is the short-circuit (grounded) pin location; candidate.
    feed_point_mm is the feed location, its z giving the pin height (falls
    back to IFA_HEIGHT_MM if 0). If the two collapse to the same (x, y) --
    true of the current frontend candidate generator, which has no
    separate short-point field -- the short pin is nudged IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM
    away so CSXCAD gets two distinct conductors. The radiating arm runs
    from the short pin, continuing past it (away from the feed) for
    length_mm.
    """
    import numpy as np
    openems_env.setup()
    from CSXCAD import ContinuousStructure
    from openEMS import openEMS

    board = device.get("board", {}) if device else {}
    # board thickness/stackup is unused here -- bare PEC ground plane only
    # until step 6 (dielectrics from the Blender export) fills it in.
    board_w, board_l, _ = board.get("size_mm") or [100.0, 50.0, 1.6]

    f_low = band.f_low_ghz * 1e9
    f_high = band.f_high_ghz * 1e9
    f0 = (f_low + f_high) / 2.0
    # The Gaussian excitation must stay broadband even when the *reported*
    # band is narrow (progress_simulation.md chose a narrow GPS-L1 sweep
    # for a fast first pass). A narrow excitation pulse is LONG in the time
    # domain and makes the FDTD run slower, not faster -- narrowing the
    # reported band is a post-processing lever (fewer CalcPort frequency
    # points), not an excitation one. Reuse the ~0.5 f0/fc ratio from
    # openEMS's own Simple_Patch_Antenna tutorial rather than deriving fc
    # from the (possibly very narrow) band width.
    fc = 0.5 * f0

    h = candidate.feed_point_mm[2] if candidate.feed_point_mm[2] > 0 else IFA_HEIGHT_MM
    short_xy = np.array(candidate.position_mm[:2], dtype=float)
    feed_xy = np.array(candidate.feed_point_mm[:2], dtype=float)

    # Arm direction is derived from the board, not from the feed/short
    # vector: it points from the board centre through the short pin,
    # continued outward-to-inward reversed (i.e. from the short pin toward
    # the board interior). Deriving it from feed-short instead (as a first
    # cut did) is circular once short/feed collapse to one point below --
    # the nudge direction would silently become the arm direction too, and
    # for an edge-placed candidate that can point the arm straight off the
    # board into free space.
    center = np.array([board_w / 2.0, board_l / 2.0])
    outward = short_xy - center
    if np.linalg.norm(outward) < 1e-6:
        outward = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
    arm_dir = -outward / np.linalg.norm(outward)
    perp_unit = np.array([-arm_dir[1], arm_dir[0]])

    if np.allclose(short_xy, feed_xy):
        # Candidate has no dedicated short-point field. The feed MUST land
        # on the arm's centreline (offset along arm_dir, toward the open
        # end) so its top actually touches the arm conductor -- an offset
        # perpendicular to the arm (a first cut did this) leaves the feed
        # pin's top floating in free space next to the arm, not on it,
        # which drives nothing: the port sees near-total reflection at
        # every frequency (this is exactly what the first real run showed:
        # S11 flat at -0.05 dB, VSWR 314, across the whole band).
        feed_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM

    open_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * candidate.length_mm
    perp = perp_unit * (IFA_ARM_WIDTH_MM / 2.0)

    mesh_div = 10.0 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 20.0
    mesh_res_mm = (C0 / f_high / 1e-3) / mesh_div         # lambda/N at f_high
    margin_mm = (C0 / f_low / 1e-3) / 4.0                  # >= lambda/4 at f_low

    NrTS = 15000 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 30000
    FDTD = openEMS(NrTS=NrTS, EndCriteria=1e-4)
    FDTD.SetGaussExcite(f0, fc)
    FDTD.SetBoundaryCond([sim.boundary] * 6)

    CSX = ContinuousStructure()
    FDTD.SetCSX(CSX)
    mesh = CSX.GetGrid()
    mesh.SetDeltaUnit(1e-3)  # working unit: mm

    mesh.AddLine('x', [-margin_mm, board_w + margin_mm])
    mesh.AddLine('y', [-margin_mm, board_l + margin_mm])
    # Explicit lines at 0 and h: the pins/arm (h = a few mm) are much
    # smaller than mesh_res_mm (tens of mm), so the general lambda/N mesh
    # alone would never place a line at the pin-top height -- the whole
    # pin would fall inside one coarse z-cell with no line bracketing its
    # top, which is exactly what caused the lumped port to fail to snap
    # to the grid ("Dimension is: 0") on the first run of this geometry.
    mesh.AddLine('z', [-margin_mm, 0, h, h + margin_mm])

    # metal_edge_res inserts extra lines flanking each conductor edge (the
    # openEMS "thirds rule" refinement) -- without it, AddEdges2Grid only
    # adds a line exactly at the primitive's own boundary, which is not
    # enough to bracket a zero-width pin/port with usable cells either.
    edge_res = mesh_res_mm / 2.0

    ground = CSX.AddMetal('ground')
    ground.AddBox(priority=10, start=[0, 0, 0], stop=[board_w, board_l, 0])
    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=ground, metal_edge_res=edge_res)

    short_pin = CSX.AddMetal('short_pin')
    short_pin.AddBox(priority=10,
                      start=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], 0],
                      stop=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], h])
    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=short_pin, metal_edge_res=edge_res)

    arm = CSX.AddMetal('radiator_arm')
    arm.AddBox(priority=10,
               start=[short_xy[0] - perp[0], short_xy[1] - perp[1], h],
               stop=[open_xy[0] + perp[0], open_xy[1] + perp[1], h])
    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=arm, metal_edge_res=edge_res)

    port = FDTD.AddLumpedPort(1, 50, [feed_xy[0], feed_xy[1], 0],
                               [feed_xy[0], feed_xy[1], h],
                               'z', 1.0, priority=5, edges2grid='xy')

    mesh.SmoothMeshLines('all', mesh_res_mm, 1.4)

    nf2ff = FDTD.CreateNF2FFBox()

    sim_path = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix=f"openems_{candidate.candidate_id}_")

    return FDTDStructure(FDTD=FDTD, port=port, nf2ff=nf2ff, sim_path=sim_path)

"""Runs the FDTD solve and extracts S-parameter data at the port."""
from __future__ import annotations

from .models import Band, FDTDStructure, SimOptions


def run_fdtd(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band, sim: SimOptions) -> FDTDStructure:
    """Step 5: run the FDTD solve, then CalcPort over the band's
    frequency window (sim.freq_points samples across
    [band.f_low_ghz, band.f_high_ghz]) to populate S-parameter data on
    structure.port. This is the slow step -- typically minutes even at
    sim.mesh_res == "coarse"; see progress_simulation.md step 7 for the
    runtime knobs.
    """
    import numpy as np
    structure.FDTD.Run(structure.sim_path, verbose=3, cleanup=True)

    n = max(sim.freq_points, 3)
    freq = np.linspace(band.f_low_ghz * 1e9, band.f_high_ghz * 1e9, n)
    structure.port.CalcPort(structure.sim_path, freq)
    structure.freq = freq
    return structure

"""Turns solved port/nf2ff data into the SimResult metrics dict."""
from __future__ import annotations

from .models import Band, FDTDStructure


def postprocess(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band) -> dict:
    """Step 5: S11 curve -> resonant_ghz / bandwidth_mhz / vswr /
    s11_min_db from the port data solve.run_fdtd() populated.
    peak_gain_dbi and efficiency need an NF2FF run at the resonant
    frequency (radiated vs. accepted power); sar_w_per_kg stays 0.0 until
    a tissue phantom exists.
    """
    import numpy as np
    port = structure.port
    freq = structure.freq

    s11 = port.uf_ref / port.uf_inc
    s11_db = 20.0 * np.log10(np.abs(s11))
    s11_curve = [{"f_ghz": float(f / 1e9), "s11_db": float(db)}
                 for f, db in zip(freq, s11_db)]

    i_min = int(np.argmin(s11_db))
    s11_min_db = float(s11_db[i_min])
    resonant_ghz = float(freq[i_min] / 1e9)
    gamma = min(float(np.abs(s11[i_min])), 0.999)
    vswr = (1.0 + gamma) / (1.0 - gamma)

    below = s11_db <= band.s11_db_max
    bandwidth_mhz = float((freq[below].max() - freq[below].min()) / 1e6) if below.any() else 0.0

    efficiency = 0.0
    peak_gain_dbi = -99.0
    if s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max:
        # Coarse angular grid for speed; nf2ff needs a resonance to probe.
        theta = np.arange(-180.0, 180.0, 10.0)
        phi = np.array([0.0, 90.0])
        nf2ff_res = structure.nf2ff.CalcNF2FF(structure.sim_path, freq[i_min], theta, phi)
        p_rad = float(nf2ff_res.Prad[0])
        p_acc = float(port.P_acc[i_min])
        if p_acc > 0:
            efficiency = max(0.0, min(1.0, p_rad / p_acc))
        dmax_db = float(nf2ff_res.Dmax[0])
        peak_gain_dbi = dmax_db + 10.0 * np.log10(efficiency) if efficiency > 0 else dmax_db - 99.0

    meets = s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max and efficiency >= band.efficiency_min

    return {
        "s11_curve": s11_curve,
        "s11_min_db": s11_min_db,
        "resonant_ghz": resonant_ghz,
        "bandwidth_mhz": bandwidth_mhz,
        "efficiency": efficiency,
        "peak_gain_dbi": peak_gain_dbi,
        "vswr": vswr,
        "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0,  # stub -- needs a tissue phantom, see progress_simulation.md step 5
        "meets_requirements": meets,
        "notes": f"resonance {resonant_ghz:.4f} GHz, S11 {s11_min_db:.1f} dB"
                 + ("" if meets else " (below thresholds)"),
    }

"""The sim workstream's single entry point.

    run_simulation(config: dict) -> dict

Contract is fixed by frontend/src/lib/types.ts (Candidate / BandRequirement /
DeviceSpec in, SimResult out) so a FastAPI endpoint can call this directly
(`from rf import run_simulation` or `from rf.run_simulation import
run_simulation`) and frontend/src/lib/runner.ts's resultFor() can swap the
mock simulate() for a real HTTP call to that endpoint without changing shape
on either side.

Solver: openEMS (FDTD), installed in rf/.venv from the vendored Windows
wheels (rf/vendor/openEMS/python/*.whl — see rf/requirements.txt and
rf/openems_env.py, which geometry.py runs before `import CSXCAD` / `import
openEMS`). geometry.build_ifa_geometry / solve.run_fdtd / postprocess.
postprocess are a real bare-PEC IFA-over-ground-plane solve, not a stub —
but step 2 (run an UNMODIFIED openEMS tutorial and check it against its own
documented result) still hasn't happened, so nothing here is cross-checked
against a known-good number yet. See rf/progress_simulation.md for the
step-by-step plan and rf/bench_scaling.py / rf/validate_dipole.py for the
PyNEC cross-check oracle (step 4) this geometry is meant to agree with.

Run as `python -m rf.run_simulation` from the repo root (needs the package
context for the relative imports below to resolve).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import time

from .device import load_device
from .geometry import build_ifa_geometry
from .models import Band, Candidate, SimOptions, SimResult
from .postprocess import postprocess
from .solve import run_fdtd


def run_simulation(config: dict) -> dict:
    """Single entry point the FastAPI backend calls. See
    rf/progress_simulation.md for the config/result contract (mirrors
    frontend/src/lib/types.ts Candidate/BandRequirement -> SimResult)."""
    t0 = time.time()
    cand = Candidate(**config["candidate"])
    band = Band(**{k: config["band"][k] for k in
                   ("id", "f_low_ghz", "f_high_ghz", "s11_db_max", "efficiency_min")
                   if k in config["band"]})
    sim = SimOptions(**config.get("sim", {}))
    device = load_device(config)

    try:
        structure = build_ifa_geometry(cand, band, device, sim)
        port_result = run_fdtd(structure, band, sim)
        metrics = postprocess(port_result, band)
        result = SimResult(
            candidate_id=cand.candidate_id,
            status="complete",
            runtime_s=time.time() - t0,
            **metrics,
        )
    except NotImplementedError as e:
        result = SimResult(
            candidate_id=cand.candidate_id,
            status="failed",
            runtime_s=time.time() - t0,
            s11_curve=[], s11_min_db=0.0, resonant_ghz=0.0, bandwidth_mhz=0.0,
            efficiency=0.0, peak_gain_dbi=0.0, vswr=0.0, sar_w_per_kg=0.0,
            meets_requirements=False, notes=f"not runnable yet: {e}",
        )
    return result.to_dict()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tutorial checkpoint (step 2/4): bare IFA over a 100x50mm ground plane,
    # no dielectrics, narrowed GPS L1 sweep (1565-1585 MHz) chosen in
    # progress_simulation.md for a fast first pass.
    demo_config = {
        "candidate": {
            "candidate_id": "gps_l1_ifa_demo",
            "antenna_type": "IFA",
            "position_mm": [95, 25, 0],
            "feed_point_mm": [95, 25, 5],
            "length_mm": 42.6,
            "orientation": "edge",
        },
        "band": {"id": "gps_l1", "f_low_ghz": 1.565, "f_high_ghz": 1.585,
                  "s11_db_max": -8, "efficiency_min": 0.45},
        "device": {"board": {"size_mm": [100, 50, 1.6]}},
        "sim": {"mesh_res": "coarse", "boundary": "MUR", "freq_points": 11},
    }
    import json
    print(json.dumps(run_simulation(demo_config), indent=2))

## Module layout

`rf/` was one file (`run_simulation.py`) through the first working version;
split on 2026-08-22 once it had three real classes of content mixed
together (data shapes, geometry construction, solver mechanics) plus a
sibling tool (`blend_loader/`) that a colleague is going to keep building
on:

```
rf/
├── __init__.py        # `from rf import run_simulation`
├── models.py           # Candidate, Band, SimOptions, SimResult, FDTDStructure, IFA_* constants
├── device.py            # load_device() — reads blend_loader-produced device.json
├── geometry.py           # build_ifa_geometry()
├── solve.py               # run_fdtd()
├── postprocess.py         # postprocess()
├── run_simulation.py      # run_simulation() orchestrator + __main__ CLI demo
├── openems_env.py         # unchanged — DLL-path setup
├── validate_dipole.py      # unchanged — PyNEC oracle
├── bench_scaling.py        # unchanged — PyNEC oracle
├── vendor/                 # unchanged, gitignored — vendored openEMS build
├── .venv/                  # unchanged, gitignored
└── blend_loader/            # moved from top-level backend/, renamed (see above)
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── load_blend.py
    ├── requirements.txt     # bpy
    ├── .venv/                # gitignored — separate bpy env, python -m rf.blend_loader.load_blend
    └── out/                  # generated device.json + STLs, gitignored
```

All sibling modules use plain relative imports (`from .models import ...`).
That means invocation is **always `python -m rf.<module>`**, never
`python rf/<module>.py` directly — the latter doesn't set up the package
context the relative imports need.

7	def run_fdtd(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band, sim: SimOptions) -> FDTDStructure:
8	    """Step 5: run the FDTD solve, then CalcPort over the band's
9	    frequency window (sim.freq_points samples across
10	    [band.f_low_ghz, band.f_high_ghz]) to populate S-parameter data on
11	    structure.port. This is the slow step -- typically minutes even at
12	    sim.mesh_res == "coarse"; see progress_simulation.md step 7 for the
13	    runtime knobs.
14	    """
15	    import numpy as np
16	    structure.FDTD.Run(structure.sim_path, verbose=3, cleanup=True)
17	
18	    n = max(sim.freq_points, 3)
19	    freq = np.linspace(band.f_low_ghz * 1e9, band.f_high_ghz * 1e9, n)
20	    structure.port.CalcPort(structure.sim_path, freq)
21	    structure.freq = freq
22	    return structure

1	"""Turns solved port/nf2ff data into the SimResult metrics dict."""
2	from __future__ import annotations
3	
4	from .models import Band, FDTDStructure
5	
6	
7	def postprocess(structure: FDTDStructure, band: Band) -> dict:
8	    """Step 5: S11 curve -> resonant_ghz / bandwidth_mhz / vswr /
9	    s11_min_db from the port data solve.run_fdtd() populated.
10	    peak_gain_dbi and efficiency need an NF2FF run at the resonant
11	    frequency (radiated vs. accepted power); sar_w_per_kg stays 0.0 until
12	    a tissue phantom exists.
13	    """
14	    import numpy as np
15	    port = structure.port
16	    freq = structure.freq
17	
18	    s11 = port.uf_ref / port.uf_inc
19	    s11_db = 20.0 * np.log10(np.abs(s11))
20	    s11_curve = [{"f_ghz": float(f / 1e9), "s11_db": float(db)}
21	                 for f, db in zip(freq, s11_db)]
22	
23	    i_min = int(np.argmin(s11_db))
24	    s11_min_db = float(s11_db[i_min])
25	    resonant_ghz = float(freq[i_min] / 1e9)
26	    gamma = min(float(np.abs(s11[i_min])), 0.999)
27	    vswr = (1.0 + gamma) / (1.0 - gamma)
28	
29	    below = s11_db <= band.s11_db_max
30	    bandwidth_mhz = float((freq[below].max() - freq[below].min()) / 1e6) if below.any() else 0.0
31	
32	    efficiency = 0.0
33	    peak_gain_dbi = -99.0
34	    if s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max:
35	        # Coarse angular grid for speed; nf2ff needs a resonance to probe.
36	        theta = np.arange(-180.0, 180.0, 10.0)
37	        phi = np.array([0.0, 90.0])
38	        nf2ff_res = structure.nf2ff.CalcNF2FF(structure.sim_path, freq[i_min], theta, phi)
39	        p_rad = float(nf2ff_res.Prad[0])
40	        p_acc = float(port.P_acc[i_min])
41	        if p_acc > 0:
42	            efficiency = max(0.0, min(1.0, p_rad / p_acc))
43	        dmax_db = float(nf2ff_res.Dmax[0])
44	        peak_gain_dbi = dmax_db + 10.0 * np.log10(efficiency) if efficiency > 0 else dmax_db - 99.0
45	
46	    meets = s11_min_db <= band.s11_db_max and efficiency >= band.efficiency_min
47	
48	    return {
49	        "s11_curve": s11_curve,
50	        "s11_min_db": s11_min_db,
51	        "resonant_ghz": resonant_ghz,
52	        "bandwidth_mhz": bandwidth_mhz,
53	        "efficiency": efficiency,
54	        "peak_gain_dbi": peak_gain_dbi,
55	        "vswr": vswr,
56	        "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0,  # stub -- needs a tissue phantom, see progress_simulation.md step 5
57	        "meets_requirements": meets,
58	        "notes": f"resonance {resonant_ghz:.4f} GHz, S11 {s11_min_db:.1f} dB"
59	                 + ("" if meets else " (below thresholds)"),
60	    }

"""Turns raw solver output into things a human can look at: the E-field
time-domain dump (SimOptions.dump_fields=True, see geometry.py) into a GIF
of the wave leaving the feed, and the S11 curve into a PNG. Nothing here is
part of the run_simulation() contract -- both are opt-in, human-facing
extras, called from the __main__ demo in run_simulation.py.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path


def render_field_animation(
    sim_path: str,
    out_gif: str | None = None,
    dump_name: str = "Et",
    geometry_mm: dict | None = None,
    max_frames: int = 100,
    fps: int = 12,
) -> str:
    """Reads <sim_path>/<dump_name>.h5 (openEMS time-domain E-field dump,
    written when geometry.build_ifa_geometry ran with sim.dump_fields=True)
    and renders |E| on the antenna's xy-plane as an animated GIF.

    openEMS's HDF5 dump layout (empirically confirmed, not documented in
    the Python bindings): /FieldData/TD/<8-digit-timestep> holds one
    (3, nz, ny, nx) array per dumped step (Ex/Ey/Ez; already decimated in
    time by the engine -- a 15000-step run wrote 251 frames, no manual
    stride needed), and /Mesh/x,y,z hold the (non-uniform, SmoothMeshLines)
    grid coordinates in metres.
    """
    import h5py
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib
    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation, PillowWriter

    h5_path = Path(sim_path) / f"{dump_name}.h5"
    if not h5_path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"{h5_path} not found -- was this structure built with "
            "SimOptions(dump_fields=True)?"
        )

    with h5py.File(h5_path, "r") as f:
        x_mm = f["Mesh/x"][:] * 1e3
        y_mm = f["Mesh/y"][:] * 1e3
        keys = sorted(f["FieldData/TD"].keys(), key=int)
        stride = max(1, len(keys) // max_frames)
        keys = keys[::stride]
        timesteps = [int(k) for k in keys]
        # (3, nz, ny, nx) -> |E| on the single z-layer this dump box covers.
        frames = np.stack(
            [np.sqrt((f["FieldData/TD"][k][:] ** 2).sum(axis=0))[0] for k in keys]
        )

    # Robust scale: the feed cell's near-field is orders of magnitude above
    # the radiating field: without normalizing, the whole rest of the wave
    # is invisible.
    vmax = float(np.percentile(frames, 99.0)) or float(frames.max()) or 1.0

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
    # imshow assumes a uniform grid, but SmoothMeshLines' spacing is not --
    # a cheap distortion trade for a much simpler/faster per-frame update
    # than pcolormesh's flattened-array bookkeeping. Fine for "briefly see
    # the wave move," not for reading off exact positions.
    im = ax.imshow(
        frames[0], origin="lower", cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=vmax,
        extent=[x_mm.min(), x_mm.max(), y_mm.min(), y_mm.max()],
        aspect="equal", animated=True,
    )
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="|E| (V/m, near-field-clipped scale)")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (mm)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y (mm)")
    title = ax.set_title("")

    if geometry_mm:
        bw, bl = geometry_mm["board_w"], geometry_mm["board_l"]
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, 0), bw, bl, fill=False,
                                    edgecolor="cyan", linewidth=1.2))
        sx, sy = geometry_mm["short_xy"]
        ox, oy = geometry_mm["open_xy"]
        fx, fy = geometry_mm["feed_xy"]
        ax.plot([sx, ox], [sy, oy], color="lime", linewidth=2, label="IFA arm")
        ax.plot(fx, fy, marker="o", color="white", markersize=5, label="feed")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.5)

    def update(i):
        im.set_data(frames[i])
        title.set_text(f"timestep {timesteps[i]}")
        return im, title

    anim = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(frames), interval=1000 / fps)
    out_gif = out_gif or str(Path(sim_path) / "field_animation.gif")
    anim.save(out_gif, writer=PillowWriter(fps=fps))
    plt.close(fig)
    return out_gif


def render_s11_plot(s11_curve: list[dict], band, out_png: str) -> str:
    """Quick S11-vs-frequency PNG from postprocess.postprocess()'s
    s11_curve, with the pass/fail threshold and target band marked."""
    import matplotlib
    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    freqs_ghz = [p["f_ghz"] for p in s11_curve]
    s11_db = [p["s11_db"] for p in s11_curve]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    ax.plot(freqs_ghz, s11_db, marker="o", markersize=3)
    ax.axhline(band.s11_db_max, color="red", linestyle="--",
               label=f"S11 threshold ({band.s11_db_max} dB)")
    ax.axvspan(band.f_low_ghz, band.f_high_ghz, color="green", alpha=0.1,
               label=f"{band.id} band")
    ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (GHz)")
    ax.set_ylabel("S11 (dB)")
    ax.set_title("Return loss")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(out_png, dpi=130)
    plt.close(fig)
    return out_png

# rf/ — EM simulation workstream

Determines whether an antenna placement candidate works, by actually
running an FDTD solve (openEMS) on an IFA-over-ground-plane geometry and
reporting S11 / resonance / bandwidth / gain / efficiency. One entry point:

```python
from rf import run_simulation
result = run_simulation(config)  # dict in -> dict out, see contract below
```

No server code lives here — a FastAPI backend (built separately) is meant
to import `run_simulation` directly. For the *why* behind every decision
below (antenna type, band, solver choice, bugs found and fixed, open
questions) see **`progress_simulation.md`** — this file is just the map.

## Quickstart

```sh
# from the repo root
rf/.venv/Scripts/python -m rf.run_simulation
```

Runs a demo GPS-L1 IFA candidate end-to-end (~2 min) and prints the
`SimResult` JSON. First time, set up the venvs per "Setup" below.

## Module layout

```
rf/
├── __init__.py         # `from rf import run_simulation`
├── models.py            # Candidate, Band, SimOptions, SimResult, FDTDStructure, IFA_* constants
├── device.py             # load_device() — reads blend_loader-produced device.json
├── geometry.py            # build_ifa_geometry() — CSXCAD/openEMS structure for one candidate
├── solve.py                # run_fdtd() — runs the solve, CalcPort over the band
├── postprocess.py           # postprocess() — port data -> SimResult metrics
├── visualize.py               # render_field_animation() / render_s11_plot() — human-facing, opt-in
├── run_simulation.py           # run_simulation() orchestrator + __main__ CLI demo
├── openems_env.py               # DLL-path setup openEMS/CSXCAD need on Windows before import
├── requirements.txt              # numpy/h5py/matplotlib/cython + vendored openEMS/CSXCAD wheels
├── vendor/                        # gitignored — vendored openEMS build (~150MB, see Setup)
├── .venv/                          # gitignored — openEMS venv
└── blend_loader/                    # separate tool + venv: .blend -> device.json (has bpy)
    ├── load_blend.py
    ├── requirements.txt              # bpy
    ├── .venv/                         # gitignored
    └── out/                            # generated device.json + STLs, gitignored
```

All modules use relative imports (`from .models import ...`), so invocation
is **always `python -m rf.<module>`**, never `python rf/<module>.py`.

## Setup

```sh
# openEMS venv
py -3.11 -m venv rf/.venv
mkdir -p rf/vendor
curl -L -o rf/vendor/openEMS_v0.0.36.zip \
  https://github.com/thliebig/openEMS-Project/releases/download/v0.0.36/openEMS_v0.0.36.zip
unzip -q -o rf/vendor/openEMS_v0.0.36.zip -d rf/vendor/
cd rf && .venv/Scripts/pip install -r requirements.txt   # cwd matters: wheel paths are relative to this file
cd .. && rf/.venv/Scripts/python -m rf.openems_env       # smoke test: imports CSXCAD + openEMS

# blend_loader venv (separate — needs bpy, not openEMS)
py -3.11 -m venv rf/blend_loader/.venv
rf/blend_loader/.venv/Scripts/pip install -r rf/blend_loader/requirements.txt
```

## Config / result contract

Mirrors `frontend/src/lib/types.ts` (snake_case), so a `run_simulation`
output can drop straight into `frontend/src/lib/runner.ts` in place of the
mock `simulate()`:

```jsonc
// in
{
  "candidate": {"candidate_id": "c001", "antenna_type": "IFA",
                "position_mm": [5,35,4], "feed_point_mm": [5,33,4],
                "length_mm": 26, "orientation": "edge"},
  "band": {"id": "gps_l1", "f_low_ghz": 1.565, "f_high_ghz": 1.585,
           "s11_db_max": -8, "efficiency_min": 0.45},
  "device": { ... },  // types.ts DeviceSpec; board/enclosure/components
  "sim": {"mesh_res": "coarse", "boundary": "MUR", "freq_points": 21,
          "dump_fields": false}  // see Visualizing below
}
```

```jsonc
// out — matches types.ts SimResult exactly
{
  "candidate_id": "c001", "status": "complete", "runtime_s": 240,
  "s11_curve": [{"f_ghz": 1.565, "s11_db": -3.1}, ...],
  "s11_min_db": -12.4, "resonant_ghz": 1.5754, "bandwidth_mhz": 18,
  "efficiency": 0.52, "peak_gain_dbi": 1.8, "vswr": 1.65,
  "sar_w_per_kg": 0.0, "meets_requirements": true, "notes": "..."
}
```

## Visualizing a run

`SimOptions.dump_fields=True` (off by default — adds solver overhead and
disk I/O) makes `geometry.py` write a time-domain E-field dump, and
`run_simulation()` renders it to a GIF, adding `field_animation_path` to
the result dict:

```python
config["sim"]["dump_fields"] = True
result = run_simulation(config)
result["field_animation_path"]  # GIF of |E| spreading out from the feed
```

`visualize.render_s11_plot(s11_curve, band, out_png)` turns any
`postprocess()` output into a return-loss PNG (threshold + target band

The command is:

```sh
cd challenge   # repo root
rf/.venv/Scripts/python -m rf.run_simulation
```

**Why this command specifically:**
- It must run as `-m rf.run_simulation` (a module inside the `rf` package), not `python rf/run_simulation.py` directly — the file uses relative imports (`from .models import ...`) that only resolve when Python has the package context, which `-m` gives it.
- It uses `rf/.venv/Scripts/python`, the openEMS-specific venv (not `rf/blend_loader/.venv`, which has `bpy` instead).

**What it does when it runs**, from `rf/run_simulation.py`'s `__main__` block:
1. Builds a demo GPS-L1 IFA candidate config, with `sim.dump_fields = True`.
2. `run_simulation(config)` runs the full pipeline: builds the CSXCAD/openEMS geometry, runs the FDTD solve (~2 min), computes S11/VSWR/resonance.
3. Because `dump_fields=True`, `geometry.py` had added an E-field time-domain dump box on the antenna's plane; `run_simulation()` then calls `visualize.render_field_animation()` on that dump and adds `field_animation_path` (a GIF) to the result.
4. The script prints the result JSON, then separately renders `rf/s11_demo.png` (S11-vs-frequency plot) via `visualize.render_s11_plot()`.

**What the two outputs show:**
- **`field_animation.gif`** — |E|-field magnitude as a heatmap on the xy-plane through the antenna, frame per (decimated) FDTD timestep. Cyan rectangle = ground plane/board edge, lime line = the IFA radiating arm, white dot = the feed point. You watch the pulse launch from the feed and spread outward.
- **`s11_demo.png`** — S11 (dB) vs. frequency across the swept band, with the pass/fail threshold (red dashed line) and the target GPS-L1 band (green shaded region) marked, so you can see at a glance whether/where it dips below threshold.

Since I already ran it earlier in this conversation, the file already exist at `rf/field_animation_demo.gif` and `rf/s11_demo.png` — I sent both to you above. Re-running with the command above regenerates fresh copies (a new run each time, ~2 min).

8	def load_device(config: dict) -> dict:
9	    """If device.manifest_path is set, it points at a device.json written
10	    by rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py (bpy runs there, in its own venv,
11	    against a .blend + materials.json sidecar — see
12	    rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py and progress_simulation.md step 6). This
13	    function only reads that JSON; it never imports bpy, so the openEMS
14	    side stays out of the bpy venv. Inline device fields (if any) are
15	    layered on top of the loaded manifest.
16	    """
17	    device = config.get("device", {})
18	    manifest_path = device.get("manifest_path")
19	    if not manifest_path:
20	        return device
21	    manifest = json.loads(Path(manifest_path).read_text())
22	    return {**manifest, **{k: v for k, v in device.items() if k != "manifest_path"}}

content.text:
## What I did

1. **Fixed a real bug first.** `rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py` assumed the axe fixture's `materials.json` schema (`material_vocabulary_used` + a `parts` list). The iPhone fixture uses a different schema (`materials: {key: {em_from_vocabulary: {...}}}`, no `parts` list — identity comes purely from object naming). Under the old code every one of the 191 iPhone parts silently got `eps_r`/`sigma_S_per_m` = `None`. Fixed to check both schemas; re-verified the axe fixture still resolves correctly (no regression).

2. **Loaded the iPhone model**: `rf/blend_loader/out/apple_iphone_15_pro/device.json` — 191 parts, all with materials resolved, one STL each. Computed the real footprint from the model's own combined bbox: **71.45 × 146.6mm** (matches the public 6.1" iPhone 15 Pro spec).

3. **Ran the same GPS-L1 IFA candidate**, resized to that real footprint, top-edge placement (short pin near the top edge, arm running down into the board). Sent the field GIF + S11 plot above.

## Result — with a caveat

S11 came in at **-9.8dB across the whole swept band** (passes the -8dB threshold) and VSWR ~1.96 — much better than the earlier 100×50mm run. But **efficiency is only ~0.2%** and peak gain is -26.8dBi, so `meets_requirements` is still `false`.

The honest caveat: the solver log shows `Max. number of timesteps was reached before the end-criteria of -40dB was reached` — it hit the 15000-step cap without fully decaying, so this didn't fully converge (unlike the earlier smaller-board run, which did reach -44dB). That undermines trust in the S11/efficiency numbers here specifically, not just as "untuned" but as "possibly not settled yet." If you want a trustworthy number for this board size, `SimOptions.mesh_res`/`NrTS` need bumping up for this geometry rather than reading this result as-is.

Also worth remembering: this still doesn't consume the iPhone's real materials — `geometry.py` only reads `board.size_mm`, so it's still a bare-PEC ground plane, just the right size now. The loaded `device.json` (191 parts, real dielectrics/conductors) is sitting there ready for step 6 (wiring materials into the FDTD build) but isn't used yet.
is it using the dielectric material property? and does it work with any blender object of a phone or laptop or is it hard coded to the input data? answer only without coding

**Dielectrics: no.** `geometry.py`'s `build_ifa_geometry()` only reads `device["board"]["size_mm"]` to draw one flat PEC (perfect-conductor) rectangle as the ground plane. It never touches `device["parts"]`, which is where the loaded `eps_r`/`sigma_S_per_m` per part actually live. So the materials you saw resolve correctly in `device.json` (glass, FR4, battery, titanium band, etc.) are loaded and sitting in the manifest, but the FDTD solve currently ignores all of them — everything except the ground plane/pin/arm is air. This is exactly the open "step 6" item in `progress_simulation.md`, not done yet.

**Generalization: partially.**

- The *loading* layer (`load_blend.py`) is genuinely generic — it walks every mesh object, parses the `<node_path>__<material_key>` naming convention, reads whichever `materials.json` schema variant is given (I fixed it to handle both today), computes bboxes, exports STLs. It'll work on any `.blend` that follows that naming + sidecar-JSON convention, phone or laptop or otherwise — not hardcoded to the iPhone or the axe specifically.
- The *solve* layer (`geometry.py`) is not shape-aware at all. It doesn't consume the per-part STLs or bounding boxes to build real device geometry — it just draws a flat rectangle sized by whatever `board.size_mm` you hand it. For the iPhone run, I computed that footprint (71.45 × 146.6mm) by hand from the loaded bboxes and passed it in manually — nothing in the pipeline derives board size automatically from a `device.json` yet. So it "works" on any device's manifest only in the trivial sense that you can compute and supply a board size for it; it doesn't yet read or adapt to a device's actual shape, layers, or materials.
consume the real materials

I'll implement this — wiring the loaded per-part `eps_r`/`sigma_S_per_m`/`mu_r` into the FDTD geometry as real dielectric/lossy materials, not just a bare PEC ground plane. Let me first confirm the exact CSXCAD material API.

20	    primitives, fed by an openEMS lumped port. Bare PEC only, no
21	    dielectrics yet -- that's step 6, once device['components'] carries
22	    real material data from a Blender export (rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py).
23	
24	    Geometry convention (see IFA_* constants in models.py): candidate.
25	    position_mm is the short-circuit (grounded) pin location; candidate.
26	    feed_point_mm is the feed location, its z giving the pin height (falls
27	    back to IFA_HEIGHT_MM if 0). If the two collapse to the same (x, y) --
28	    true of the current frontend candidate generator, which has no
29	    separate short-point field -- the short pin is nudged IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM
30	    away so CSXCAD gets two distinct conductors. The radiating arm runs
31	    from the short pin, continuing past it (away from the feed) for
32	    length_mm.
33	    """
34	    import numpy as np
35	    from . import openems_env
36	    openems_env.setup()
37	    from CSXCAD import ContinuousStructure
38	    from openEMS import openEMS
39	
40	    board = device.get("board", {}) if device else {}
41	    # board thickness/stackup is unused here -- bare PEC ground plane only
42	    # until step 6 (dielectrics from the Blender export) fills it in.
43	    board_w, board_l, _ = board.get("size_mm") or [100.0, 50.0, 1.6]
44	
45	    f_low = band.f_low_ghz * 1e9
46	    f_high = band.f_high_ghz * 1e9
47	    f0 = (f_low + f_high) / 2.0
48	    # The Gaussian excitation must stay broadband even when the *reported*
49	    # band is narrow (progress_simulation.md chose a narrow GPS-L1 sweep
50	    # for a fast first pass). A narrow excitation pulse is LONG in the time
51	    # domain and makes the FDTD run slower, not faster -- narrowing the
52	    # reported band is a post-processing lever (fewer CalcPort frequency
53	    # points), not an excitation one. Reuse the ~0.5 f0/fc ratio from
54	    # openEMS's own Simple_Patch_Antenna tutorial rather than deriving fc
55	    # from the (possibly very narrow) band width.
56	    fc = 0.5 * f0
57	
58	    h = candidate.feed_point_mm[2] if candidate.feed_point_mm[2] > 0 else IFA_HEIGHT_MM
59	    short_xy = np.array(candidate.position_mm[:2], dtype=float)
60	    feed_xy = np.array(candidate.feed_point_mm[:2], dtype=float)
61	
62	    # Arm direction is derived from the board, not from the feed/short
63	    # vector: it points from the board centre through the short pin,
64	    # continued outward-to-inward reversed (i.e. from the short pin toward
65	    # the board interior). Deriving it from feed-short instead (as a first
66	    # cut did) is circular once short/feed collapse to one point below --
67	    # the nudge direction would silently become the arm direction too, and
68	    # for an edge-placed candidate that can point the arm straight off the
69	    # board into free space.
70	    center = np.array([board_w / 2.0, board_l / 2.0])
71	    outward = short_xy - center
72	    if np.linalg.norm(outward) < 1e-6:
73	        outward = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
74	    arm_dir = -outward / np.linalg.norm(outward)
75	    perp_unit = np.array([-arm_dir[1], arm_dir[0]])
76	
77	    if np.allclose(short_xy, feed_xy):
78	        # Candidate has no dedicated short-point field. The feed MUST land
79	        # on the arm's centreline (offset along arm_dir, toward the open
80	        # end) so its top actually touches the arm conductor -- an offset
81	        # perpendicular to the arm (a first cut did this) leaves the feed
82	        # pin's top floating in free space next to the arm, not on it,
83	        # which drives nothing: the port sees near-total reflection at
84	        # every frequency (this is exactly what the first real run showed:
85	        # S11 flat at -0.05 dB, VSWR 314, across the whole band).
86	        feed_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * IFA_SHORT_GAP_MM
87	
88	    open_xy = short_xy + arm_dir * candidate.length_mm
89	    perp = perp_unit * (IFA_ARM_WIDTH_MM / 2.0)
90	
91	    mesh_div = 10.0 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 20.0
92	    mesh_res_mm = (C0 / f_high / 1e-3) / mesh_div         # lambda/N at f_high
93	    margin_mm = (C0 / f_low / 1e-3) / 4.0                  # >= lambda/4 at f_low
94	
95	    NrTS = 15000 if sim.mesh_res == "coarse" else 30000
96	    FDTD = openEMS(NrTS=NrTS, EndCriteria=1e-4)
97	    FDTD.SetGaussExcite(f0, fc)
98	    FDTD.SetBoundaryCond([sim.boundary] * 6)
99	
100	    CSX = ContinuousStructure()
101	    FDTD.SetCSX(CSX)
102	    mesh = CSX.GetGrid()
103	    mesh.SetDeltaUnit(1e-3)  # working unit: mm
104	
105	    mesh.AddLine('x', [-margin_mm, board_w + margin_mm])
106	    mesh.AddLine('y', [-margin_mm, board_l + margin_mm])
107	    # Explicit lines at 0 and h: the pins/arm (h = a few mm) are much
108	    # smaller than mesh_res_mm (tens of mm), so the general lambda/N mesh
109	    # alone would never place a line at the pin-top height -- the whole
110	    # pin would fall inside one coarse z-cell with no line bracketing its
111	    # top, which is exactly what caused the lumped port to fail to snap
112	    # to the grid ("Dimension is: 0") on the first run of this geometry.
113	    mesh.AddLine('z', [-margin_mm, 0, h, h + margin_mm])
114	
115	    # metal_edge_res inserts extra lines flanking each conductor edge (the
116	    # openEMS "thirds rule" refinement) -- without it, AddEdges2Grid only
117	    # adds a line exactly at the primitive's own boundary, which is not
118	    # enough to bracket a zero-width pin/port with usable cells either.
119	    edge_res = mesh_res_mm / 2.0
120	
121	    ground = CSX.AddMetal('ground')
122	    ground.AddBox(priority=10, start=[0, 0, 0], stop=[board_w, board_l, 0])
123	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=ground, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
124	
125	    short_pin = CSX.AddMetal('short_pin')
126	    short_pin.AddBox(priority=10,
127	                      start=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], 0],
128	                      stop=[short_xy[0], short_xy[1], h])
129	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=short_pin, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
130	
131	    arm = CSX.AddMetal('radiator_arm')
132	    arm.AddBox(priority=10,
133	               start=[short_xy[0] - perp[0], short_xy[1] - perp[1], h],
134	               stop=[open_xy[0] + perp[0], open_xy[1] + perp[1], h])
135	    FDTD.AddEdges2Grid(dirs='xy', properties=arm, metal_edge_res=edge_res)
136

138	                               [feed_xy[0], feed_xy[1], h],

def _add_device_materials(CSX, parts: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Step 6: one CSXCAD material per distinct material_key in
    device['parts'] (from rf/blend_loader/load_blend.py's device.json），
    one AddBox per part. bbox_mm-only -- the STLs load_blend.py exported
    aren't imported as polyhedra; a phone-scale part count (~200) of full
    AddPolyhedronReader calls would blow the runtime budget geometry.py
    otherwise keeps bounded via margin_mm/mesh_res for a coarse first
    pass. Priority 1: strictly below the antenna's own PEC primitives
    (priority 10) and port (priority 5), so a device part can never mask
    the antenna geometry it's meant to sit alongside.

    A device manifest's coordinates are Blender-native (centred on the
    object); the ground plane/antenna above are corner-anchored at
    [0, board_w] x [0, board_l]. Coordinates here are shifted so the
    parts' own combined bbox starts at (0, 0, 0), aligning the two.
    There's no collision-avoidance with the antenna itself (e.g. against
    a battery or frame segment sharing its cell) -- that's on
    candidate.keepout_mm / placement choice, not this function.
    """
    usable = [p for p in parts if p.get("bbox_mm") and p.get("eps_r") is not None]
    if not usable:
        return

    xs = [c[0] for p in usable for c in p["bbox_mm"]]
    ys = [c[1] for p in usable for c in p["bbox_mm"]]
    zs = [c[2] for p in usable for c in p["bbox_mm"]]
    ox, oy, oz = -min(xs), -min(ys), -min(zs)

    materials: dict[str, object] = {}
    for p in usable:
        key = p.get("material_key") or "unknown"
        mat = materials.get(key)
        if mat is None:
            mat = CSX.AddMaterial(f"device_{key}")
            mat.SetMaterialProperty(
                epsilon=p["eps_r"],
                kappa=p.get("sigma_S_per_m") or 0.0,
                mue=p.get("mu_r") or 1.0,
            )
            materials[key] = mat
        (x0, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z1) = p["bbox_mm"]
        mat.AddBox(priority=1,
                   start=[x0 + ox, y0 + oy, z0 + oz],
                   stop=[x1 + ox, y1 + oy, z1 + oz])

## Done — the FDTD solve now consumes the real materials

`geometry.py` gained `_add_device_materials()`: whenever `device["parts"]` is present (loaded from a `blend_loader` manifest), it adds one real CSXCAD material per distinct `material_key` (`epsilon=eps_r`, `kappa=sigma_S_per_m`, `mue=mu_r`) and one box per part, positioned by shifting the parts' own combined bbox to align with the antenna's coordinate frame. It runs automatically — no new option to set.

Verified against the real iPhone 15 Pro asset (191 parts): S11 shifted from **-9.8dB (bare PEC) to -7.5dB (with real materials)** — the dielectrics/lossy metal are demonstrably loading the antenna, not inert. Sent updated GIF/plot above.

**Two honest limitations, documented in `progress_simulation.md` and `rf/README.md`:**
- **bbox-only** — each part becomes one axis-aligned box with that material, not its real mesh shape (importing ~200 actual STL meshes as polyhedra would blow the runtime budget).
- **No collision-awareness** — nothing checks whether a device part (battery, frame) overlaps the antenna geometry at the chosen placement.

Also fixed a real bug hit along the way: `load_blend.py` assumed the axe fixture's `materials.json` schema and silently returned `eps_r=None` for all 191 iPhone parts, which use a different (but equally valid) schema. Fixed to handle both; re-verified the axe fixture is unaffected.

does the simulation find the right location of the antenna, explain the simulation script as if I am 13 years old

**Short answer: no.** Right now the simulation doesn't search for a good spot — it only *grades* one spot that a human (me, in this case) typed in by hand. I picked "top edge, centered" for the iPhone run myself; nothing in the code tried other positions and compared them. To actually *find* the best location, someone would need to write a loop that calls this simulation many times with different `position_mm` values and picks the one with the best S11/efficiency — that loop doesn't exist yet in `rf/`.

Now, the script explained like you're 13:

---

**The big idea:** Radio waves are invisible ripples, like waves in a pool. If you want to know whether an antenna works well, you can either build it for real and test it with expensive lab equipment, or you can make a *computer pretend* to be the lab — that's what this whole thing does.

**Step 1 — Build a tiny LEGO version of the antenna and the phone.** (`geometry.py`)
The computer chops up 3D space into a grid of tiny boxes, like Minecraft blocks. It places:
- A flat metal sheet (the "ground plane" — think of it as the phone's metal skeleton)
- A bent metal wire antenna sticking up off of it (the IFA — shaped like a backwards "F")
- A little "feed point" where we're going to zap it with energy, like plugging in a battery
- Now with the real iPhone data: a bunch of boxes of different materials all around — glass, battery, metal frame — each one told "you're glass, so waves slow down and bend a little inside you" or "you're metal, so waves bounce off you."

**Step 2 — Zap it and watch the ripples.** (`solve.py`)
The computer sends a tiny pulse of energy into the feed point — like flicking the surface of a pool once — and then, block by block, tiny time-step by tiny time-step, calculates how the ripple spreads to each neighboring block. It does this thousands of times per second of simulated time. This is the slow, expensive part (the actual "physics math").

**Step 3 — Read the results.** (`postprocess.py`)
After the ripple settles down, the computer checks: how much of the energy we put in came *back* out (bounced back = wasted, bad) versus how much left the antenna as a real radio wave (radiated = good). From that it calculates numbers like:
- **S11** — how much energy bounced back (want this very negative, like -8dB or lower)
- **VSWR** — a similar "how well is it matched" score (want close to 1)
- **Efficiency** — what fraction of the energy actually became a useful radio wave
- **Resonant frequency** — the frequency this antenna shape "likes" best

**Step 4 — Package it up.** (`run_simulation.py`)
This is the "front door" — one function that does steps 1-3 in order and hands back a tidy dictionary of results, so a website can display them without knowing any of the physics.

**Bonus — Watch the ripple as a movie.** (`visualize.py`)
If you turn on `dump_fields`, the computer saves a snapshot of the ripple every so often and stitches the snapshots into a GIF — that's the animation I sent you, the wave spreading out from the feed point across the board.

**What it does *not* do yet:** try lots of different antenna spots and tell you which one is best. It's a "grader," not yet a "search engine."
